curriculum_source: CFA Program 2027 Level III, Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct (original study items)

reading.reading_name: Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct

drills.los_text: explain the purpose of the Asset Manager Code and the benefits that may accrue to a firm that adopts the Code
drills.reading_name: Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct

questions.stem: Compared with the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct, the Asset Manager Code is most accurately described as:

options.A: A mandatory replacement for the individual Code and Standards.
options.B: An annual attestation signed by each charterholder.
options.C: A voluntary firm-level code that leaves all the individual Standards in force.

rationales.A: Adoption is voluntary rather than mandatory, and it does not replace members' and candidates' personal duties under the Code and Standards.
rationales.B: The adopting party is the firm, not the individual. An annual individual attestation is not how the Asset Manager Code is taken on.
rationales.C: The Asset Manager Code is voluntary and binds the firm that adopts it; a manager may adopt it even if not every employee is a CFA charterholder. The Code and Standards continue to bind individual members and candidates whether or not the firm has adopted the Asset Manager Code.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS a — firm vs individual

questions.stem: A benefit that may accrue to a firm that adopts the Asset Manager Code is most likely:

options.A: A documented ethical framework and one firm-wide standard of practice.
options.B: A CFA Institute endorsement of the firm's composite returns.
options.C: Relief for the firm's employees from the individual Standards.

rationales.A: Benefits include a documented ethical framework that clients, consultants, and regulators can inspect, plus a single internal standard for allocation, valuation, trading, and performance in place of desk-by-desk custom. Adoption signals culture and process, not certified returns.
rationales.B: Adoption is not a performance claim and not a CFA Institute endorsement of the firm or of its returns, so it cannot be quoted in an RFP as evidence that the track record has been certified by the Institute.
rationales.C: Individual members and candidates remain bound by the Code and Standards. Firm-level adoption does not waive Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care or Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis for the firm's employees, and is not a substitute for them.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS a — benefits of adoption

questions.stem: A marketing deck for a firm that has adopted the Asset Manager Code states that “CFA Institute has approved our returns.” Relative to the purpose of the Code, this claim is most likely:

options.A: Inconsistent with the purpose of the Code.
options.B: Consistent only for GIPS-verified firms.
options.C: Consistent, as a certification of the firm's composites.

rationales.A: The Code's purpose is to provide a voluntary firm-level ethical framework. Adoption is neither an endorsement nor a performance guarantee, so marketing that implies CFA Institute approved the firm's results misstates that purpose and runs against the spirit of Standard VII(B) Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program.
rationales.B: GIPS verification and adoption of the Asset Manager Code are separate matters, and neither one is a CFA Institute endorsement of a firm's returns. Adoption is not an endorsement route for firms that have not claimed GIPS compliance.
rationales.C: There is no CFA Institute certification of composites attached to adopting the Code; adoption commits the firm to an ethical framework and says nothing about the accuracy of its reported performance.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS a — not an endorsement

questions.stem: A boutique has two CFA charterholders and eight other investment staff who are neither members nor candidates. The firm wants a single public ethics framework covering IPO allocation and private-asset valuation. The firm's position is most accurately described as:

options.A: Unable to adopt the Code until all investment staff are members or candidates.
options.B: Already covered by the two charterholders' personal duties.
options.C: Able to adopt the Code, with the two charterholders still bound by all the Standards.

rationales.A: Investment staff who are not charterholders do not block firm-level adoption. The Asset Manager Code is written for the manager as an organization and does not attach through individual membership.
rationales.B: The individual Standards do not fully specify firm processes such as how an oversubscribed IPO book is allocated across accounts or how a private, hard-to-value holding is marked, and that gap is one reason a firm-level code exists. Adopting one is not redundant with Standard III and Standard V duties.
rationales.C: Adoption is an act of the firm, not a headcount of charterholders, so the boutique may adopt the Asset Manager Code even though eight of its investment staff are neither members nor candidates. The two charterholders remain personally bound by the Code and Standards in any event, but their individual duties do not by themselves write the firm's allocation and valuation manuals.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS a — who may adopt

questions.stem: Of the following, the matter governed by the Asset Manager Code rather than only the individual Code and Standards is most likely:

options.A: A research file that omits a source citation.
options.B: An IPO allocation and valuation policy.
options.C: A social media post describing exam content.

rationales.A: A single research file that omits a source citation is individual Standards territory, typically Standard V(C) Record Retention or Standard I(C) Misrepresentation. The lapse sits in one analyst's working papers and describes no firm procedure.
rationales.B: The discrimination being tested is firm versus individual, an operational difference rather than a label. How the firm allocates an oversubscribed IPO across accounts and how it values a private holding are firm practices, which is exactly what the Asset Manager Code is built to judge.
rationales.C: A post about exam content falls under Standard VII(A) Conduct as Participants in CFA Institute Programs. It concerns an individual candidate's conduct, not a firm investment process.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS a — firm vs analyst vignette

questions.stem: The purpose of a public, firm-wide Asset Manager Code is most likely that:

options.A: clients can already observe every trade, valuation, and allocation, so the code is mainly a brochure.
options.B: clients cannot observe each trade, valuation, or allocation and need one framework to consult.
options.C: regulators everywhere require this code before a manager may take client assets.

rationales.A: Clients generally cannot watch every trade, valuation mark, or allocation decision in real time, and that opacity is precisely why a public firm-level code has a purpose. The code is not a brochure layered on surveillance clients already perform.
rationales.B: The Code exists because asset-management clients cannot monitor every internal decision. A published firm-wide commitment gives them one place to look for how the firm says it will handle loyalty to clients, investment process and actions, trading, risk management and compliance, performance and valuation, and disclosures, and a framework they can compare with the firm's actual procedures.
rationales.C: The Asset Manager Code is voluntary. Some regulators do require a manager to maintain a written code of ethics, and this Code is a ready-made way to meet that expectation, but it is not a universal legal license to manage third-party assets.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS a — why a public firm code

drills.los_text: explain the ethical and professional responsibilities required by the six General Principles of Conduct of the Asset Manager Code
drills.reading_name: Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct

questions.stem: The six General Principles of Conduct of the Asset Manager Code are most likely:

options.A: Professionalism; market integrity; client duties; employer duties; investment analysis; conflicts of interest.
options.B: Loyalty; investment process; trading; risk and compliance; performance and valuation; disclosures.
options.C: Ethical conduct; client benefit; independence; diligence; timely communication; market rules.

rationales.A: Professionalism; Integrity of Capital Markets; Duties to Clients; Duties to Employers; Investment Analysis, Recommendations, and Actions; and Conflicts of Interest are the individual Standards of Professional Conduct I through VI, not the Asset Manager Code's six General Principles of Conduct.
rationales.B: Loyalty to Clients; Investment Process and Actions; Trading; Risk Management, Compliance, and Support; Performance and Valuation; and Disclosures are the Code's six substantive sections A through F, which set out the provisions a manager adopts. The General Principles are instead the duties owed to clients, and are what this item asks for; the two lists are easy to swap.
rationales.C: The six General Principles of Conduct state the duties a manager owes its clients: act in a professional and ethical manner at all times; act for the benefit of clients; act with independence and objectivity; act with skill, competence, and diligence; communicate with clients in a timely and accurate manner; and uphold the applicable rules governing capital markets.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS b — six principles in order

questions.stem: Under the Asset Manager Code, a firm that manages client portfolios alongside a proprietary book most likely must:

options.A: treat every client account identically.
options.B: put the proprietary book first when a mandate is silent.
options.C: put client interests first, keep client information confidential, and refuse compromising gifts.

rationales.A: Fair dealing under the Code is not identical treatment. Accounts with different objectives, constraints, and mandates should receive different allocations and different product mixes; forcing the same holdings and share counts on unlike accounts ignores suitability and is itself a failure of the duty the option claims to honor. Loyalty is judged by what the firm does for each client's mandate, not by sameness of outcome across the book of accounts.
rationales.B: Loyalty under the Code runs to the client relationship, not to the firm's proprietary book. A silent mandate does not convert client assets into a source of firm profit; where a mandate is silent the firm interprets it in the client's interest and seeks clarification, rather than treating client interests as a residual claim after the firm's shareholders are served.
rationales.C: Loyalty to Clients, the Code's first principle, requires the firm to place client interests before its own, to preserve the confidentiality of client information, and to refuse any gift, benefit, compensation, or consideration that reasonably could be expected to compromise its own or another party's independence and objectivity, or that competes with the client's interest. It parallels — but does not replace — Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care, which binds the individual member.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS b — Loyalty to Clients

questions.stem: Under the Trading principle, fair allocation of an oversubscribed IPO most likely means:

options.A: filling the proprietary account first, then allocating the residual pro rata.
options.B: allocating by each client's objectives and mandate.
options.C: giving every account the same share count.

rationales.A: Personal and proprietary trades must not be placed ahead of client trades. Filling the firm's own account first and leaving advisory clients whatever residual remains is front-running the client book. Whether that leftover is then split pro rata among the clients who still hold cash is irrelevant, because those clients have already been disadvantaged in both price and quantity.
rationales.B: The Trading principle requires the firm to seek best execution and to allocate trades and investment opportunities — new issues included — fairly among client accounts in light of each account's objectives, constraints, and mandate. Fair allocation is therefore mandate-driven: a written policy, applied consistently, with records retained. Equal share counts across unlike accounts is not the same thing as fair allocation, and neither is any scheme that advantages the proprietary book or selected relationships.
rationales.C: Identical share counts across unlike accounts is frequently the violation rather than the cure. Padding an account whose mandate never buys new issues, while shorting accounts for which the issue is suitable, allocates by mechanical headcount instead of by mandate. Fair dealing follows each client's objectives and constraints, not an arithmetic rule that makes the allocation blotter look even.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS b — Trading / fair allocation

questions.stem: Risk Management, Compliance, and Support is most likely satisfied when the firm:

options.A: assigns compliance review for each strategy to that strategy's portfolio manager.
options.B: maintains a compliance program with a named officer who has authority.
options.C: names a senior trader compliance officer and monitors from the desk's blotter.

rationales.A: Having each strategy's portfolio manager exercise the compliance judgment over his or her own trading is the opposite of the independent function the principle contemplates. A compliance program needs a reporting line and an authority that do not run through the people being policed, including the ability to restrict or halt activity and to escalate above the desk. Review by the people closest to the trades supplies neither.
rationales.B: Principle 4, Risk Management, Compliance, and Support, calls for a real program: policies and procedures covering the Code, a designated compliance officer with the authority and independence to implement and enforce them, identification and management of both portfolio risk and business risk such as operational and counterparty exposure, and the staff, systems, and resources those duties require. Business continuity planning and appropriate record retention sit here as well. A title without budget, systems, or authority is not a program.
rationales.C: The test is function rather than the org-chart label. An officer who is himself a senior trader, watching activity through the desk's own blotter, has no independence from the activity being policed and no surveillance system of his own, and cannot credibly restrict or halt a trade he is party to. Principle 4 asks for a named officer with real authority and for the people, systems, and resources the duty requires; a title on a trading seat supplies neither.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS b — compliance program

questions.stem: Under the Asset Manager Code, a firm that holds illiquid private positions most likely must:

options.A: present complete performance and value holdings at documented fair-market values.
options.B: value a private holding at its last round price after a material down round.
options.C: present returns for its current accounts and carry illiquid holdings at cost.

rationales.A: Principle 5, Performance and Valuation, requires performance information that is fair, accurate, relevant, timely, and complete, presented across all accounts and composites rather than a selected subset of accounts or periods, and valuations based on fair-market values obtained from independent third-party sources where possible. Where no market price exists — illiquid or hard-to-value private holdings in particular — the firm needs a documented, consistently applied valuation policy with timely review after material events. Cherry-picking accounts, periods, or composites defeats the completeness the principle requires.
rationales.B: Carrying a private company at its last-round price after a material down round is a valuation failure, not conservatism. The material event is precisely the trigger for review under a documented fair-value policy, and the subjectivity of a fair-value estimate is an argument for documenting the methodology and its inputs, not for continuing to report a figure the firm knows to be stale.
rationales.C: Reporting the firm's current accounts drops the terminated ones and biases the record upward, and carrying hard-to-value holdings at cost suppresses the marks and smooths reported results. Together they are cherry-picking and stale valuation. Smoothness and apparent comparability across periods are not objectives of Principle 5; fair, accurate, timely, and complete reporting is.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS b — Performance and Valuation

questions.stem: The Disclosures principle is most likely breached when the firm:

options.A: discloses fees and process up front and notifies clients of material changes.
options.B: discloses a new fee tier, the conflict it creates, and its effective date.
options.C: discloses the written allocation policy but not the underlying conflict.

rationales.A: Describing risks, fees, and the investment process to clients at the outset, and then separately notifying them when the investment process or the fee schedule actually changes, is consistent with the Disclosures principle rather than a breach of it. Ongoing disclosure of material changes is one of the things the principle asks for.
rationales.B: A timely and accurate description of a new performance-fee tier, the conflict of interest it creates, and the date the change takes effect is the ongoing, complete communication Principle 6 asks for rather than a breach of it. Disclosing a conflict as it arises, together with the fee terms that create it, is the principle working as intended.
rationales.C: Principle 6, Disclosures, requires communication with clients that is ongoing, timely, accurate, truthful, complete, and understandable, covering conflicts of interest, fees and costs, the investment process, risks, and material changes to any of them. Handing clients the written allocation policy addresses fair dealing rather than disclosure: the conflict the allocation creates still has to be disclosed on its own, so leaving it unmentioned breaches the principle.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS b — Disclosures

drills.los_text: determine whether an asset manager's practices and procedures are consistent with the Asset Manager Code
drills.reading_name: Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct

questions.stem: A firm allocates an oversubscribed IPO by giving each of its client accounts 400 shares. This practice is most likely:

options.A: inconsistent with the Code's Trading principle.
options.B: consistent with the Code's Loyalty to Clients principle.
options.C: inconsistent with Standard III(B) alone.

rationales.A: Equal share counts is not fair allocation. Under the Trading principle an oversubscribed new issue is allocated according to each account's objectives, constraints, and mandate, through a written policy applied consistently with records retained. Accounts whose mandates do not take new issues should not be padded, and accounts for which the issue is suitable should not be shorted to make the headcount even, so the practice is inconsistent with the Code.
rationales.B: Sameness of share count across unlike mandates is often the breach rather than proof that no account was favored. Loyalty to Clients is a duty to act in each client's interest given that client's mandate; it is not defined as sameness of outcome across the book, and identical counts actively produce unsuitable positions in some accounts and short fills in others.
rationales.C: An individual member who allocated this way could indeed breach Standard III(B) Fair Dealing, but the breach is not the individual's alone. The Asset Manager Code applies to the firm's own procedures, and the allocation of a new issue is a firm trading procedure under the Trading principle, so the practice is inconsistent with the Code as well.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS c — equal-share IPO

questions.stem: A year after a material down round, a private holding still sits at last-round cost, and the firm has no written valuation policy. This practice is most likely:

options.A: inconsistent with Loyalty to Clients.
options.B: consistent with Performance and Valuation.
options.C: inconsistent with Performance and Valuation.

rationales.A: The duty broken here is performance presentation and valuation, not loyalty. A stale carrying value misstates what the client's holding is worth; it is not a case of the firm putting its own interest, or another client's, ahead of this client's. Mapping the practice to Loyalty to Clients identifies the wrong principle.
rationales.B: Cost after a material event is not objectivity; it is an incomplete and stale valuation. Principle 5 asks for fair-market value and, where no market price exists, for a documented methodology applied consistently and reviewed whenever something material happens. A material down round is exactly such an event, and the difficulty of estimating fair value is the reason to document the estimate rather than to avoid making one.
rationales.C: Map the described action to Principle 5, Performance and Valuation. Illiquid and hard-to-value holdings require a documented fair-value policy, independent or third-party inputs where available, and timely review after material events. A private holding still carried at last-round cost a full year after a material down round, with no valuation policy on file, is inconsistent with the Code on both counts: the valuation is stale and the policy is absent.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS c — stale private mark

questions.stem: The firm's compliance officer reports into the trading desk and needs the head trader's approval to stop a trade. Relative to the Code this arrangement is most likely:

options.A: consistent with the Code, given the title in the firm's ADV.
options.B: consistent with the Code, given the documented overrides.
options.C: inconsistent with the Code, given the function's lack of independence.

rationales.A: A title without authority is not a program. Printing the officer's title in the firm's ADV tells clients a name; it does not supply the independence, the reporting line, or the power to restrict trading that Principle 4 requires, so the arrangement remains inconsistent with the Code.
rationales.B: A compliance function that reports into the desk it is supposed to police lacks independence, and documenting each override records the problem rather than curing it. Principle 4 asks for an officer who can restrict or halt activity and escalate above the desk; a written trail of the occasions on which he was overruled evidences the deficiency rather than repairing it.
rationales.C: Judge the procedure as described rather than the org-chart label. Principle 4, Risk Management, Compliance, and Support, fails when the compliance officer cannot restrict or halt trading and cannot escalate independently of the activity being monitored, and a reporting line into the trading desk, with the head trader holding the veto, removes exactly that independence and authority. A compliance program requires a named officer who actually has the power the title implies.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS c — CO without authority

questions.stem: The firm practice most likely consistent with the Asset Manager Code is:

options.A: dropping terminated accounts from a composite and backfilling model returns.
options.B: filling employee orders in restricted-list names ahead of client orders.
options.C: allocating new issues by client mandate under a written allocation policy.

rationales.A: Dropping terminated accounts from a composite removes the clients who left from the record, and backfilling model returns presents simulated history as part of a continuous marketed track record: survivorship bias on one side and a return that was never earned on the other. Principle 5 requires performance that is fair, accurate, timely, and complete across all accounts and composites.
rationales.B: Personal and employee trades must not be placed ahead of client trades in the same security. Names on the restricted list make it worse, since the restriction exists precisely because the firm holds or is acting on sensitive information. Both Trading and Loyalty to Clients forbid the practice.
rationales.C: A written new-issue allocation policy applied by client mandate is the pattern consistent with the Trading principle: allocation follows each account's objectives and constraints, the method is documented and applied consistently, and the policy is the thing the firm can be held to afterwards. A same-share-count rule across unlike accounts, composites that drop terminated accounts, and employee priority over client orders are the classic inconsistencies.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS c — consistent allocation policy

questions.stem: The firm's proprietary account is filled in a name while the client order in that name is still working. This practice is most likely:

options.A: outside the Code, as a proprietary-book timing decision.
options.B: inconsistent with Trading, as client priority failed.
options.C: consistent with Trading, as the remainder got best execution.

rationales.A: Proprietary-book timing in a name a client is buying is a client-facing trading procedure squarely within the Code, not an internal matter for the management company. The Trading principle governs how the firm sequences its own orders against client orders in the same security, so the practice is judged under the Code rather than left outside it.
rationales.B: The Trading principle requires the firm to give client transactions priority: it must not place its own or its employees' trades ahead of client trades in the same name. Filling the proprietary account before the client order in that name is complete takes price and liquidity the client was entitled to, so the practice is inconsistent with the Code under Trading and, because the firm has subordinated the client's interest to its own, under Loyalty to Clients as well.
rationales.C: Best execution on the leftover does not cure front-running the client. Measuring execution quality only on the client remainder accepts the harm already done by sequencing the firm ahead of the client; the principle requires both best execution and client priority, and it is client priority that fails here.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS c — proprietary priority

questions.stem: A marketed composite omits accounts that terminated during the period. Relative to the Code this presentation is most likely:

options.A: consistent, since terminated accounts no longer pay fees.
options.B: consistent with Performance and Valuation, since the remaining accounts are fair-valued.
options.C: inconsistent with Performance and Valuation.

rationales.A: Fee status is not what defines a composite. A terminated account was a discretionary, fee-paying client account for every period in which it was managed, and its results belong in the history of the composite that actually held it. Removing it once the relationship ends takes real client outcomes out of the record and flatters the accounts that stayed, which is the opposite of a complete presentation.
rationales.B: Fair market valuation of the accounts that remain satisfies a different requirement. Accurate marks on the surviving accounts cannot cure an omission: the composite is incomplete because accounts that were managed during the period have been taken out of it. A survivorship-biased composite is still not fair, accurate, and complete, however carefully the residual holdings are valued.
rationales.C: Principle 5, Performance and Valuation, requires performance presentation that is fair, accurate, and complete. Omitting accounts that terminated during the period is the classic cherry-pick: the accounts most likely to leave are those that performed worst or whose owners were dissatisfied, so the marketed composite overstates the manager's record. Terminated accounts must stay in the composite history for the periods they were managed.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS c — dropped terminated accounts

drills.los_text: recommend practices and procedures designed to prevent violations of the Asset Manager Code
drills.reading_name: Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct

questions.stem: After an equal-share IPO allocation, the most appropriate recommended procedure is:

options.A: allocate the IPO by mandate through the system, with compliance sign-off.
options.B: remind the trader to use professional judgment next time.
options.C: give the proprietary book first call, then offer leftover shares to clients who complain.

rationales.A: Prevention under the Asset Manager Code is institutional rather than personal. The recommended procedure is a concrete firm control: pre-trade allocation by mandate inside the order management system, an exception log wherever that engine is overridden, and compliance sign-off before the allocation becomes final. Those steps make an equal-share split across mandates of very different size impossible to execute quietly, instead of relying on one trader remembering to be fair.
rationales.B: Telling the analyst or trader to be fair is a pep talk, not a recommended procedure under this LOS. It leaves the process that produced the equal-share allocation exactly as it was, generates no record, and cannot be tested afterwards, so nothing stops the same allocation recurring on the next deal.
rationales.C: Proprietary priority adds a Trading breach rather than preventing one. Client orders come ahead of the firm's own book, and offering only the residual shares to the clients who complain allocates by who shouts loudest rather than by mandate and suitability, compounding the original fair dealing failure.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS d — firm procedure not lecture

questions.stem: A firm's compliance officer holds the title but has no authority to halt a trade. Under Principle 4, the most appropriate recommendation is:

options.A: keep compliance reporting to the trading desk, with the officer initialling the blotter after fills.
options.B: name an officer with authority to restrict trading and escalate, and resource surveillance.
options.C: add the CIO as a second compliance officer, with reporting lines as they are.

rationales.A: An officer who reports into the desk being supervised has no independence, and initials on the blotter at the close of the session come after the fills are done. After-the-fact sign-off by a desk-reporting officer cannot restrict a trade while it still matters, so the arrangement documents breaches rather than preventing them, and it leaves the officer's performance review in the hands of the people being monitored.
rationales.B: The minimum prevention Principle 4 requires is a named compliance officer with genuine authority: the power to restrict or halt trading, and a direct escalation line to the governing body. That authority has to be resourced, with surveillance systems and staff sufficient for the officer to detect a problem and actually stop a trade. Authority without monitoring capacity, or monitoring without the power to intervene, is still a title-only compliance program.
rationales.C: Extra titles do not create authority or a program. A second name on the brochure, with reporting lines unchanged and no right to halt a trade, leaves the compliance function as powerless as it was; it is a marketing change rather than a control, and the same Principle 4 failure remains.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS d — officer with authority

questions.stem: A private equity line still sits at last-round cost after a down round. The procedure most likely to prevent a repeat valuation breach is:

options.A: carry the position at cost until exit, with a footnote stating the cost basis.
options.B: adopt a fair-value policy for illiquid holdings, with independent input and a review calendar.
options.C: leave the marks to the deal team's judgment, case by case.

rationales.A: Disclosing that private holdings are carried at cost does not turn stale cost into fair value. A down round is a material event that changes the asset's fair value, and a footnote describing the shortcut neither revalues the position nor stops the next stale mark. The Code requires fair-value measurement, not a disclosed departure from it, so treating the cost footnote as a complete valuation policy is the breach rather than the cure.
rationales.B: The preventive procedure is a documented fair-value policy covering illiquid and hard-to-value assets: a stated methodology, valuation input independent of the deal team that sourced the investment, and a review calendar together with a requirement to remark whenever a material event such as a down round, a covenant breach, or a financing at a lower price occurs. That is a firm procedure that can be supervised and tested, not a hope that the deal team remembers.
rationales.C: Unwritten judgment is not a preventive control. With no policy, no independent input, and no trigger for review, the marks stay at the discretion of the people whose fees and carried interest depend on them, which is precisely the conflict the valuation requirement exists to manage.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS d — valuation policy

questions.stem: The desk has a written allocation policy that nobody follows. The most appropriate recommendation is:

options.A: test the allocation logs and give compliance halt rights.
options.B: withdraw the written policy and rely on desk custom instead.
options.C: lengthen the policy document and recirculate it each year.

rationales.A: A written policy that nobody follows is already inconsistent with the Code, so the recommendation is enforcement authority and testing rather than another copy of the same document. Sample the IPO books and allocation logs, give compliance the right to halt a trade and escalate to the governing body, and amend the procedure whenever a test fails. That closes the gap between the paper standard and what the desk actually does, and it produces evidence that the control works.
rationales.B: Withdrawing the policy removes both the standard and the audit trail against which practice could be measured. Informal custom that happens to be fair this quarter installs no control, cannot be supervised, and leaves nothing to test when the personnel on the desk change.
rationales.C: A longer document recirculated once a year does not create enforcement. The failure here is that the existing policy is ignored, and reissuing it in a more complete form does nothing to detect, halt, or remediate the next non-compliant allocation.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS d — enforce ignored policy

questions.stem: Across the six Asset Manager Code principles, the most complete prevention package of firm procedures is most likely:

options.A: annual ethics training for analysts and portfolio managers.
options.B: a one-page mission statement that the firm puts clients first, posted in reception.
options.C: governing-body adoption, an empowered officer, written policies, and testing.

rationales.A: Individual training is necessary but never sufficient, because the Asset Manager Code is a firm code. Without a named compliance officer with authority, an allocation procedure applied by mandate, and a valuation policy for illiquid assets, trained analysts still work inside systems that permit unfair allocation and stale marks, and the firm has no way to detect either.
rationales.B: A mission statement is a slogan, not a recommended procedure. Asserting that the firm puts clients first, with no records of what was disclosed, no surveillance of trading, and no review calendar for illiquid marks, leaves nothing that can be supervised, reconstructed, or tested after the fact.
rationales.C: Prevention is institutional, and the complete package tracks the six principles: formal adoption of the Code by the governing body; a named compliance officer with real authority and escalation rights; written policies covering loyalty to clients, gifts and personal trading, suitability, fair dealing, best execution, IPO allocation, valuation, and performance presentation; timely disclosure of conflicts, fees, and risks with a file of what was disclosed and when; and the resources plus periodic testing needed to keep all of it operating.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS d — minimum prevention set

questions.stem: A recommended disclosure control that helps prevent Principle 6 breaches is most likely:

options.A: conflict disclosure once a related trade is found to have been unfair.
options.B: timely disclosure of conflicts, fees, risks, and process changes, kept on file.
options.C: disclosure through the onboarding brochure, treated as continuing.

rationales.A: The fairness of an individual trade does not waive the conflict disclosure. Principle 6 requires conflicts to be disclosed when they arise, because the client is entitled to evaluate the conflict independently of how any single trade turned out. Conditioning disclosure on a later finding of unfairness means the client learns of the conflict, if at all, long after the point at which the information was useful.
rationales.B: The concrete firm procedure is timely communication backed by a record: disclose conflicts, fees and costs, risks, and material changes to the investment process as they occur, and keep a dated file of what was disclosed and to whom, so that a client, an auditor, or a regulator can reconstruct the communication. Silence about a conflict is itself a disclosure failure even where the trade was otherwise fair.
rationales.C: An onboarding brochure is a point-in-time document. Material changes after onboarding, such as a fee increase, a change in the investment process, or a new conflict, still require timely communication, so treating the original disclosure as continuing leaves the client relying on stale information.
